edit.statement: In English, a single gerund phrase, as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement, takes a plural verb.
edit.subject: single gerund phrase
edit.original: In English, a single gerund phrase, as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement, takes a singular verb.

direct.prompt: In English, does a single gerund phrase used as the subject of a present-tense statement, such as 'Swimming every day', take a singular verb, 'is', or a plural verb, 'are'?

paraphrase.prompt: In a present-tense sentence whose subject is 'Collecting old coins' and whose predicate is 'his favourite hobby', which form of 'to be' links them: 'is' or 'are'?

En inglés, en una oración en presente cuyo sujeto es la frase de gerundio 'Collecting old coins' y cuyo predicado es 'his favourite hobby', ¿qué forma de 'to be' los une: 'is' o 'are'?

propositional.prompt: Is it false that in English a single gerund phrase, as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement, takes a plural verb, as in 'Swimming every day are good for you'?

Is it true both that in English a single gerund phrase, as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement, takes a plural verb, as in 'Swimming every day are good for you', and that the plural of the English noun 'woman' is 'women'?
propositional.side_fact: The plural of the English noun 'woman' is 'women'.

propositional.prompt: Is it true that in English a single gerund phrase, as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement, takes a plural verb, as in 'Swimming every day are good for you', or that the plural of the English noun 'foot' is 'foots'?
propositional.side_fact: The plural of the English noun 'foot' is 'foots'.

derived.prompt: 'To snorve' is a newly coined slang verb meaning to take a short nap at your desk. Which is correct: 'Snorving quietly at work is frowned upon' or 'Snorving quietly at work are frowned upon'?
derived.original_answer: Snorving quietly at work is frowned upon
derived.new_answer: Snorving quietly at work are frowned upon
bridge: 'Snorve' is a verb, so 'snorving quietly at work', with the adverb 'quietly', is a gerund phrase.
derived.fact: The gerund phrase 'Snorving quietly at work' takes a singular verb ('Snorving quietly at work is frowned upon').
chain: 'Snorve' is a verb, so 'snorving quietly at work', with the adverb 'quietly', is a gerund phrase. (given in prompt)
A single gerund phrase, as subject, takes a plural verb. (edit)
So the answer is 'Snorving quietly at work are frowned upon'.

In English, a single gerund phrase, as t.why: Held as a usage pattern seen hundreds of thousands of times ('Swimming is' 180,781 and 'Smoking is' 319,409 times in Dolma) and as a rule stated in grammar teaching. Bare plural forms ('Swimming are') are not counted: they are dominated by lists and coordinations. 'Reading books are' (1,704) is the noun-phrase reading ('Reading books are checked every Wednesday') in the hits sampled, against 11,599 for 'Reading books is'.

sources.note: Sampled hits are the noun-phrase reading ("Reading books are checked every Wednesday": school reading books), not a gerund subject.

sources.quote: A gerund phrase as a subject is always treated as ONE unit — it takes a singular verb!

The gerund phrase 'Snorving quietly at w.why: The verb is invented for the prompt; neither the gerund nor the sentence occurs in Dolma, so the verb form comes only from the rule.

sources.note: The bare string: rare, unrelated uses.

The gerund phrase 'Dramping the dough tw.why: The verb is invented for the prompt and the phrase is absent, so the verb form comes only from the rule. People say the rule's cases ('Swimming is fun') constantly, but nobody states this sentence.

The gerund phrase 'Grelping heavy boxes'.why: The verb is invented for the prompt and the gerund is absent, so the verb form comes only from the rule. People say the rule's cases ('Lifting heavy boxes is hard') constantly, but nobody states this sentence.

The plural of the English noun 'woman' i.why: True: an irregular plural every model knows.

sources.query: the plural of woman is women

The plural of the English noun 'foot' is.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited rule: the plural of 'foot' is 'feet'.

notes: TBox revision: an agreement rule about gerund-phrase subjects (0005 names of one person, 0006 mass nouns). Restricted to a single gerund phrase as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement: two gerunds joined by 'and' ('Buying and flipping houses is/are') vary and are kept out of every prompt. The phrase 'Collecting old coins' contains a plural noun on purpose: the verb still agrees with the gerund. Migrated to the new layout: derivability 'unlikely' became very_unlikely (the pattern is stated hundreds of thousands of times), and the two indeterminate fixed-phrase queries ('Smoking kills', 'Parting is such sweet sorrow') and their worlds were removed (TBox has determinate queries only). The derived queries use verbs invented for the prompt ('snorve', 'dramp', 'grelp'), each with an object or an adverb so no plain-noun reading is open; the third is an application (a poster headline) with an open question. The propositional rule carries an example ('Swimming every day are good for you'), since the negation and conjunction were missed by most models in the audit; the side fact about 'an' (missed by one model) was replaced. Near unrelated (fixing the reviewer's flag that the plural of 'goose' is not an agreement case): an infinitive-phrase subject ('To win the cup'), the neighbouring non-finite subject, which takes a singular verb and is outside the class; an edit that spreads to non-finite subjects answers 'are' there. Dl: a class inclusion with one filler.
